As AI-mediated decisions spread across organizations, accountability is often addressed through legal liability, ethics guidelines, or ad hoc managerial responses. This paper argues that such approaches fail to capture a deeper structural problem: accountability collapses when decision authority, exception response, and responsibility are not coherently aligned. We conceptualize accountability as a protocol rather than a role or rule, and examine how responsibility becomes displaced onto individuals or functions when decision boundaries are undefined. The paper demonstrates why existing organizational roles cannot absorb this burden and why accountability must be designed as part of decision infrastructure. The chapter investigates legal principles explaining the relationship between control, foreseeability, and duty of care, along with regulatory requirements for human oversight and governance. It also examines issues related to automation bias, black-box models, and extended decision chains that involve Security Operations Centers and third parties. Through combining a legal perspective with security operational practice, the chapter outlines a system for determining responsibility, handling liability, and making defensible decisions in AI-assisted security systems.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 7, 9]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.66695/ijir.v1i1.009\", \"title\": [\"Algorithmic Decision-Making Systems and Legal Responsibility: Reconstructing Fault, Agency, and Accountability in the Digital Age\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Abstract In the digital age, algorithmic decision-making systems have become central actors in shaping legal, economic, and social outcomes. This transformation poses a fundamental challenge to classical legal concepts such as agency, fault, responsibility, and accountability, which are traditionally grounded in human intention and consciousness. While legal doctrine presumes a human decision-maker capable of intent, negligence, and moral judgment, algorithmic systems operate through opaque, data-driven processes that defy these assumptions. This article examines the […]</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.66695/ijir.v1i1.009\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6738541\", \"title\": [\"The Accountability Reconstruction Problem: Decision Traceability, Institutional Responsibility, and Defensibility in Accelerated Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p><p>Modern institutions increasingly operate through distributed computational systems, accelerated operational environments, adaptive infrastructures, and interconnected decision ecosystems. As decision velocity increases across AI-enabled and non-AI systems, institutions face growing difficulty reconstructing how consequential outcomes emerged across fragmented technological and organizational environments.</p>\\n<p>This paper introduces the Accountability Reconstruction Problem (ARP) as a structural institutional condition emerging when operational complexity exceeds institutional traceability coherence, escalation continuity, and reconstruction readiness. Drawing on current literature across cybersecurity, institutional governance, telecommunications resilience, AI systems, and organizational accountability research, the paper argues that many institutions remain operationally efficient while progressively losing the ability to reconstruct accountability continuity under consequence.</p>\\n<p>The paper explores several structural conditions increasingly associated with reconstruction fragility within accelerated environments, including decision opacity, escalation discontinuity, distributed responsibility, and contextual traceability erosion. It further examines how institutional legitimacy increasingly depends not solely on operational performance, but on whether institutions remain capable of reconstructing, explaining, and defending accountability coherence once outcomes become contested.</p>\\n<p>The paper contributes to broader discussions surrounding institutional defensibility, governance continuity, accountability under acceleration, and systemic trust within increasingly complex operational environments.</p></jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6738541\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "2415c530cfd931517f1d6010247d05a07d5c09198767fdfeded7d08406a6a0c1", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "responsibility_formation", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.6238138", "doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007", "doi:10.66695/ijir.v1i1.009", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6738541"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6238138", "https://doi.org/10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007", "https://doi.org/10.66695/ijir.v1i1.009", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6738541"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
